articles.title: Learning traps
articles.abstract: When constituents are uncertain about whether leaders' policy preferences align with their interests, policy choices generate a trade‐off between payoffs and information. Leaders can experiment with their preferred policy, but if the outcome is bad, constituents learn this and threaten office removal. I use a repeated model of political agency to analyze how this trade‐off shapes long‐lived, term‐unlimited leaders' policy choices. When there is uncertainty about the optimal policy for constituents, leaders implement “learning traps”: spatially intermediate policies that halt learning about what the best policy is. They experiment only when their preferences are very likely to be aligned with constituents, a contrast to the “gambling for resurrection” logic ubiquitous in the literature. I provide a case study that examines how the 1861 reforms ending Serfdom in Imperial Russia represented the logic of a “learning trap” and illustrate additional applications of the model to political contagion and economic policymaking.

articles.title: The threat‐enhancing effect of authoritarian power sharing
articles.abstract: Power‐sharing deals can potentially solve the autocrat's commitment problem, yet often fail to prevent conflict. This article develops a dynamic model to examine a largely overlooked friction: Sharing power within an authoritarian regime bolsters the opposition's coercive capabilities. The resultant threat‐enhancing effect creates two distinct commitment problems for the opposition, which determine if and when power sharing occurs. First, the opposition cannot commit to refrain from leveraging its enhanced threat. The ruler prefers to incur a revolt than peacefully share power if the threat‐enhancing effect is large. Second, the threat‐enhancing effect tempts the opposition to wait for a future power‐sharing deal, which undercuts the opposition's commitment to revolt today. New dynamic implications arise: delayed power sharing, conflict, or an increased willingness for the ruler to share power are all possible. Scrutinizing the opposition's limited commitment ability contrasts with the predominant existing focus on the autocrat's commitment problem.

articles.title: Globalization and the Hinterland: International Trade and the Rural–Urban Divide
articles.abstract: The growing political divide between rural and urban regions is often attributed to rural deindustrialization and import competition in manufacturing. Yet this cleavage emerged in many countries well before rural industrialization, pointing to underlying economic forces that existing accounts have overlooked. We argue that comparative advantage in agriculture is one such force: rural voters are more likely to support protectionist parties and policies when local agriculture is uncompetitive, since this sector is often central to their communities’ economic and social life. Using a new harmonized dataset of surveys from 123 countries and extensive data on voting behavior in the European Union, we find strong support for our argument. An additional analysis exploiting exogenous subnational variation in agricultural competitiveness in the United States post-NAFTA further corroborates our findings: the political divide between rural and urban voters is pronounced in uncompetitive regions but negligible in those possessing a comparative advantage in agriculture.

articles.title: Economic Self-Interest and Support for Redistribution: New Evidence Using Election Results Data
articles.authors: JIEUN LEE, E. GRANT BALDWIN, G. AGUSTIN MARKARIAN, BENJAMIN J. NEWMAN
articles.abstract: A formidable corpus of scholarship explores the role of economic self-interest in shaping public support for redistribution. One striking feature of this literature is its near-exclusive reliance on reported preferences in surveys, with little-to-no research analyzing revealed preferences in the form of actual voting on redistribution. Leveraging eight redistributive ballot initiatives across six American states and a total of 73,053 observations of revealed support for redistribution, we uncover consistent evidence that the economic standing of precinct voters is systematically related to their support for redistribution. We find that lower- to upper-middle-income precincts are each significantly more supportive of redistribution than upper-income precincts, with pronounced decreases in support associated with the increasing prevalence of high-income households subject to proposed tax increases. Finally, we observe the largest class differential in support for redistribution in more heavily Republican precincts.

articles.title: When Politics Enters the Waiting Room: Far-Right Electoral Victories Exacerbate Discrimination in Access to Healthcare
articles.authors: MERLIN SCHAEFFER, ALESSIO ROMARRI, DINA ROSENBERG, KRZYSZTOF KRAKOWSKI
articles.abstract: Far-right political shifts have been linked to increased racism, raising concerns about their impact on minority access to public services. This study investigates whether far-right electoral victories encourage discrimination by street-level bureaucrats, who are expected to act impartially. We conducted a nested research design in Italy, combining a field-experimental audit with a regression discontinuity design focused on municipalities near the electoral threshold for far-right mayors. Research assistants with native-Italian and West-African accents contacted municipal healthcare offices to request registration with a general medical practitioner. Compared to native-Italian callers, those with West-African accents faced significantly higher rates of scrutiny and dismissive responses. Leveraging close elections, we find that this disparity was exacerbated in municipalities where far-right candidates narrowly won. These findings demonstrate that far-right electoral success can undermine impartiality and equal access to essential services.

articles.title: Geoengineering, Moral Hazard, and Disrespect
articles.abstract: Scientists and policy makers are increasingly exploring solar geoengineering as a tool for combatting anthropogenic climate change. Yet these technologies have drawn intense ethical criticism. One of the most influential critiques – the ‘moral hazard’ objection – holds that pursuing solar geoengineering risks undercutting mitigation efforts; and that, as a result, governments should halt the development of solar geoengineering. This paper argues that the moral hazard objection faces a dilemma: either the proposed solution to the moral hazard effect (that is, stifling geoengineering) is unnecessary, or it expresses a morally troubling form of disrespect. Articulating this dilemma serves three purposes. It shows, first, that the moral hazard objection is substantially more difficult to vindicate than it initially appears. Second, it clarifies what would need to be shown, empirically, to overcome this ethical hurdle. Finally, and crucially, it sheds light, more broadly, on what it means to respect people’s agency when designing and implementing public policies.

articles.title: ‘The winners take it all, the losers standing small’: Party centralization and Duverger's law
articles.authors: Luís Locatelli, George Avelino, Ivan Chaves Jucá

articles.title: Motivation or ability? Explaining the effect of party polarisation on proximity voting
Estimating effective electoral thresholds
Populism and conspiracy theories: A cross-national analysis
Contested terrain: How attitudes toward gender issues relate to voting behavior
articles.abstract: While research increasingly links sexist attitudes to far-right support, public debates have moved well beyond women’s equality to encompass LGBTIQ+ rights. Yet studies have been slow to follow, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of attitudes toward trans, intersex, and non-binary people and how they associate with party choice, especially beyond far-right support. Drawing on original data from the German Social Cohesion Panel (2022/23), we are, to our knowledge, among the first to investigate a broader range of gender-related attitudes and find, first, that these constitute two empirically distinct dimensions, binary and non-heteronormative gender issues , that while conceptually intertwined, warrant separate examination. Second, while support for binary gender issues is widespread, non-heteronormative issues remain highly contested. Third, these dimensions relate differently to vote choice: attitudes toward binary gender issues show partisan sorting across the left-right spectrum, while attitudes toward non-heteronormative gender issues reveal a specific antagonism between the Greens and (center-)right parties. Finally, considering both dimensions together uncovers an asymmetry: voters of (center-)right parties form a cohesive conservative bloc, while supportive voters with different attitudinal profiles disperse across (center-)left parties.

articles.title: Gender inclusivity and perceptions of party ideology: Observational and experimental evidence
articles.authors: James Adams, David Bracken, Noam Gidron, Will Horne, Seonghui Lee, Diana O’Brien, Lie Philip Santoso, Kaitlin Senk, Randolph T. Stevenson
articles.abstract: Do citizens use gender-based heuristics to infer political parties’ ideological positions? We posit that citizens view more ‘gender inclusive’ parties as more left-leaning than comparable male-dominated organizations. Cues about gender inclusivity, moreover, come not only from women’s presence in parties’ legislative delegations but also from other visible signals of women’s incorporation into parties – including as leaders and supporters – and through organizational rules promoting women’s inclusion. We present analyses of election survey data from 21 Western publics over time, which show that, controlling for the left–right tones of parties’ manifestos, citizens perceive more gender-inclusive parties as more left-wing and that the cumulative impact of the various dimensions of gender inclusivity is substantial. We next report experimental evidence from four countries, which provides further support for gender-based heuristics. Our findings highlight the importance of not just the message but also the messenger in shaping citizens’ assessments of parties’ ideological perceptions.

articles.title: Losing the engaged without winning the disengaged: Personalism and the choice of political news
articles.abstract: When political news centers on the policy work or private lives of individual politicians rather than on parties, it can obscure the collective actors citizens must judge at elections. The usual defense is that such personalism attracts readers, especially those otherwise unlikely to choose political news. We test this claim in survey experiments in Denmark, the United Kingdom, and the United States ( N = 3039). Respondents chose between an entertainment article and a political article whose subheadline attributed a new bill to a party, an individual politician (individualized), or the politician’s personal story (privatized). Personalism recruited no readers. Effects are negative in all countries and pooled amount to a significant five percentage point loss. The losses were concentrated among politically engaged citizens, while the least engaged, the very readers personalism is meant to attract, were unmoved. Party-centered news thus entail no audience sacrifice as citizens prefer the format that keeps parties visible.

articles.title: Is sidestepping the judiciary seen as democratic? Evidence from Great Britain and Spain
articles.authors: Noam Titelman, Javier Sajuria, Lisa Zanotti
articles.abstract: Executives often bypass the courts without public backlash and, sometimes, with public support. This research note evaluates one strategy employed by politicians for securing public backing when bypassing the courts: a majoritarian framing. We evaluate this strategy through candidate survey experiments in Great Britain ( n = 957) and Spain ( n = 995) that contrast this framing with institutional checks and balances. On average, respondents rate the candidate pushing for court bypassing as less democratic. Nevertheless, a sizeable minority in both countries judges this option as more democratic. These results indicate that heterogeneous understandings of what counts as democratic can sustain public tolerance for executive bypass of the courts.

articles.title: Generalizing Causal Effects with Noncompliance: Application to Deep Canvassing Experiments
articles.abstract: Standard approaches in generalizability often focus on generalizing the intent-to-treat effect. However, in practice, a more policy-relevant quantity is the generalized impact of an intervention across compliers. While instrumental variable methods are commonly used to estimate the complier average causal effect (CACE) within samples, standard approaches cannot be applied to a target population with a different distribution from the study sample. This article makes several key contributions. First, we introduce a new set of identifying assumptions in the form of a population-level exclusion restriction that allows for identification of the target CACE (T-CACE) in both randomized experiments and observational studies. This allows researchers to identify the T-CACE without relying on standard principal ignorability assumptions. Second, we propose a class of inverse-weighted estimators for the T-CACE and derive their asymptotic properties. We provide extensions for settings in which researchers have access to auxiliary compliance information across the target population. Finally, we introduce a sensitivity analysis for researchers to evaluate the robustness of the estimators in the presence of unmeasured confounding and extend existing tests to evaluate instrument validity in this context. We illustrate our proposed method through extensive simulations and a study evaluating the impact of deep canvassing on reducing exclusionary attitudes.

articles.title: Learning from Coalition Politics: How Episodes of Increased Complexity Can Enhance Citizens’ Political Efficacy
articles.authors: Christoffer Green-Pedersen, Ida Bæk Hjermitslev, Mathias Wessel Tromborg

articles.title: Beliefs About Public Opinion and the Perceived Legitimacy of Policy Decisions
articles.abstract: Democratic legitimacy is typically thought to depend on whether political decisions reflect public opinion, or majority preferences. Do citizens share this standard? And what if citizens are wrong about public opinion? We study how beliefs about public support for controversial policy proposals are associated with the perceived legitimacy of adopting them, and whether accurate polling information changes these judgments. In a representative survey experiment in Germany, respondents reported their own position on four such proposals, estimated public support, and rated the legitimacy of adopting each one. For a random subset of proposals, respondents received accurate polling information showing that the proposal lacked majority support. We find that perceived public support predicts legitimacy judgments even after accounting for respondents’ own policy preferences. Yet these perceptions are often inaccurate and shaped by respondents’ own views. Corrective polling information modestly lowers perceived legitimacy, especially among those who initially overestimated public support. The findings suggest that misperceptions of public opinion can distort, but accurate information can also partly correct, citizens’ assessments of democratic legitimacy.

articles.title: Do Political Elites Evaluate Election Outcomes More Favourably than Citizens? Evidence from Parallel Surveys
What Drives Voter Bias Against Muslim Politicians? An Experimental Examination
articles.abstract: Religious and ethnic minorities remain underrepresented in political office, but its reasons are debated. Using administrative data from Norwegian local elections, we show that candidates with Muslim names receive fewer personal votes, and propose that this is (partly) due to political beliefs about Muslims as politicians.To examine this claim, we identify salient political beliefs and implement a conjoint experiment that estimates anti-Muslim bias with and without information on these beliefs.In a low-information setting, respondents exhibit a substantial anti-Muslim bias, but providing belief-relevant information reduces this anti-Muslim bias by 2–5 percentage points. The largest reduction occurs when respondents learn candidates’ positions on minority-rights issues. This reduction is driven by right-wing voters and is large enough to eliminate the left-right gap in anti-Muslim bias. These findings show a strong political component in the anti-Muslim bias.

articles.title: Forest governance as carceral formation: Policing and punishment in the ordinary governance of British Columbia's forests
Putting your money where your mouth is: Expressions of Chinese nationalist sentiments are not just cheap talk
articles.abstract: Do nationalist expressions reflect a willingness to pay costs or are they cheap talk? This is important because theories expect nationalism affects a wide range of outcomes that pose costs to participants, including international conflict and participation in boycotts. However, past research has either relied on self‐reports that cannot rule out cheap talk or outcome measures at higher levels of analysis, such as international trade flows, that do not directly link individual‐level nationalist sentiment to behavior. In contrast, we measure both nationalist sentiments and costly behavior on an individual level using the content of millions of Chinese social media posts and the nationality of the brand of users' devices, for example type of cellphone, as a costly behavioral measure. We find that nationalist sentiment makes citizens less likely to use US and Japanese brands with an instrumental variable analysis.

articles.title: Feeling the body politic: Interoception as a mechanism of political stress resilience
articles.abstract: Politics can substantially harm physical and mental health, especially in polarized contexts, making political polarization a major non‐medical cause of disease and suffering. We examined whether citizens can protect their health without undermining civic engagement. Across three studies with over 2000 participants during the 2022 U.S. midterms and 2024 presidential election, we show that interoceptive sensibility, that is, the ability to perceive and trust one's internal bodily signals, protects against politics' adverse health effects. Higher interoceptive sensibility consistently predicted lower emotional, physical, behavioral, and social health costs, controlling for political identity, demographics, and emotion regulation. During the charged 2024 election, it further predicted fewer negative emotions, more hope for the future, and less fear, particularly when their candidate lost. Interoceptive sensibility also correlated with political engagement and efficacy, suggesting it enhances rather than inhibits participation. Our findings highlight it as a promising trait for mitigating political stress without reducing civic involvement.

articles.title: Do “warm glow” feelings affect climate mitigation behaviors? A field experiment on consumer electric energy choices
articles.authors: Jennifer Jerit, Jason Barabas, Hwayong Shin, Molly Gahagen, Scott May
articles.abstract: Addressing the climate crisis is going to require behavioral change in many aspects of daily life. A growing literature suggests the promise of “warm glow” messaging that features the pleasure and satisfaction one experiences from acting sustainably. Yet previous research has relied almost exclusively on self‐reported behavioral intentions, leaving open whether such appeals meaningfully affect real‐world, costly choices. We partnered with a local organization to conduct a field experiment on energy choices in Hanover, New Hampshire. Using a randomized roll‐out design in early 2025, we systematically varied the timing of postcard mailers that contain a warm glow message encouraging customers to increase the renewable content of their energy option. Analyses of administrative data on consumer energy choices reveal that warm glow messages delivered in a field setting have a null effect on adoption of higher‐renewable power choices, with a small number of customers changing to the greener but more costly option. Our study provides novel behavioral evidence on the real‐world impact of intrinsic motivation appeals in the climate domain.

articles.title: Do felon voting rules affect criminal prosecutions?
articles.abstract: Felon disenfranchisement laws can alter the composition of the electorate. Accordingly, we argue that in states with such laws, elected prosecutors may be tempted to assign felon status strategically. We test our argument using criminal case data from Virginia and leveraging a sudden policy change—unexpectedly announced by the Governor on April 22, 2016—enfranchising all felons upon completion of their prison or probation sentence. Using well-known racial differences in partisanship as a measure of likely political alignment, we show that the announcement corresponded to an increase in criminal charge severity and sentence length for defendants who were politically unaligned with their prosecutors, and a decrease for aligned defendants. Evidence suggests that these changes may have been partially motivated by partisan concerns in the lead-up to the 2016 federal elections.

articles.title: Polity size and women’s representation: evidence from two large-scale boundary reforms
articles.authors: Moa Frödin Gruneau, Jan Teorell, Kåre Vernby
articles.abstract: Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women’s representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

articles.title: The cultural roots of state-owned enterprises: evidence from Europe
articles.authors: Ákos Dombi, Piotr Matuszak, Katarzyna Szarzec
articles.abstract: This paper examines the cultural roots of state ownership of enterprises. Drawing on data for European countries, we show that the scale of state ownership of enterprises is smaller in individualist societies than in collectivist ones. This relationship is robust to a broad set of cultural, economic, and historical controls. We address endogeneity concerns by using genetic, epidemiological, and linguistic data as instruments for individualism. We propose several political economy mechanisms underlying this relationship. First, in collectivist societies, voter preferences are tilted toward more extensive state ownership of enterprises. Second, in collectivist societies, interest groups may be stronger and democracy may be weaker, both of which can result in a larger share of state-owned enterprises in the economy. We provide empirical evidence supporting these channels. Finally, we show that the negative relationship between individualism and the scale of state ownership also holds in non-European countries.

articles.title: Nonviolent protest and ideological change in education: a public choice approach
articles.authors: Joshua D. Ammons, Ali Palida, Ilia Murtazashvili
articles.abstract: This paper applies a public choice framework to examine how successful nonviolent protest campaigns are associated with changes in the ideological orientation of state education systems. We conceptualize education as a site of political bargaining in which organized interests shape educational governance and classroom political socialization. Using cross-national data on political mobilization and educational ideology, we estimate the effects of successful nonviolent campaigns on nationalist, socialist-communist, and democratic ideological emphasis within classroom instruction. We find that successful nonviolent campaigns are associated with declines in nationalist and socialist-communist ideological emphasis alongside increased emphasis on democratic norms and democratic institutions. We do not interpret these shifts as movement from indoctrination to ideological neutrality. Rather, following recent work on political socialization and educational ideology, we treat all educational systems as engaged in ideological transmission and interpret the findings as shifts in the ideological orientation emphasized within educational practice. The results suggest that successful nonviolent mobilization is associated with broader political and institutional realignment that reshapes educational political socialization. Parallel estimates for successful violent campaigns do not display the same consistent pattern, although this contrast is descriptive rather than a direct test of the difference between campaign types.

articles.title: Does policy advocacy generate good PR? Evidence from labor unions and minimum wages
Judicial performance and public procurement choice
articles.authors: Alessandro Cavalieri, Alessandro Melcarne, Giovanni Battista Ramello
articles.abstract: This paper investigates whether judicial performance influences the choice of procurement procedures adopted by public authorities. Using data on Italian municipal public works contracts between 2009 and 2012, it examines the choice between negotiated procedures and formal tendering mechanisms in a range where both options were legally available. Identification relies on a spatial discontinuity design that exploits exogenous variation in judicial delay across court jurisdictions, further refined through intra-regional border comparisons and coarsened exact matching. The results show that longer judicial delays significantly reduce the likelihood of using negotiated procedures and increase the use of formal auctions. Consistent with a growing body of literature showing that inefficient courts increase contractual uncertainty, we argue that poor judicial performance shifts procurement choices toward highly formalized procurement mechanisms rather than more discretionary and market-oriented forms of contracting. In this sense, formal procurement procedures may partially compensate for weak judicial enforcement by shifting transaction governance toward greater ex-ante specification, procedural control, and verifiability. More broadly, the paper suggests that judicial ineffectiveness may contribute to the expansion of bureaucratic controls, shifting governance away from market-based arrangements and toward increasingly proceduralized administrative structures.

articles.title: Picture book of apportionment and voting difficulties
articles.abstract: The geometry associated with apportionment and voting methods enables us to “see" what difficulties will arise, why certain complexities are inevitable, how to create supporting examples, and identify similarities of the problems afflicting both areas. Although several new results become apparent, such as the harsh consequences for a method satisfying IIA and a replacement for the modified divisors that are used with monotone apportionment approaches, the emphasis is to use this picture book approach to explain why certain behaviors must happen.

articles.title: When does artificial intelligence strengthen the case for markets? Revisiting the socialist calculation debate
“Manifestly unlawful”: How US troops think about the duty to disobey illegal orders
articles.authors: Charli Carpenter, Heather Kumove, Geraldine Santoso
articles.abstract: US troops are required to disobey unlawful orders but obey lawful ones – yet social scientists know very little about how they draw that line or what drives the decision to actually disobey when it counts. We asked 818 active-duty American troops to define “manifestly unlawful orders” in their own words, as well as whether they would obey or disobey specific scenarios in which they might be asked to directly and intentionally target unarmed civilians. A majority of troops could provide clear examples of situations in which they would feel compelled to disobey orders. Of specific scenarios, over a third of US troops were prepared to disobey orders to target civilians, either with nuclear weapons or if asked to shoot civilian protesters. Controlling for gender, age, branch of service, party affiliation, voting behavior, rank, income, and education, we find simply thinking ahead about the concept of “manifestly unlawful orders” is the single biggest predictor of soldiers’ willingness to refuse to harm civilians.

articles.title: Worth a try? The electoral consequences of symbolic legislation
articles.authors: Nicole Huffman, John V. Kane, David L. Stack
articles.abstract: With the US Congress increasingly gridlocked, fewer bills are becoming law. Nevertheless, members continue to engage in what we call “symbolic legislating”—that is, introducing legislation that has effectively no chance of securing enough votes to become law. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the electoral implications of sponsoring symbolic legislation. It is possible that voters reward their legislator’s efforts to move the status quo closer to their position even if it has no chance of becoming law. On the other hand, because symbolic legislation is doomed to fail, it may decrease a legislator’s perceived effectiveness and, thus, their political support. Alternatively, it is possible that sponsoring symbolic legislation has no impact beyond a cue of the politician’s position. In this Research Article, we test these competing hypotheses using a survey experiment. Our experimental results clearly demonstrate that, assuming shared party and issue position, sponsoring symbolic legislation is strongly rewarded. Moreover, the effect is even stronger among voters who are most likely to attend to this information in the real world and operates similarly across parties.
